description:
**`-p N` is per-run, so N is a lie the moment a second repo starts.** Five `chief run` invocations across five repos share no concurrency budget and cannot see each other. Nothing coordinates them, so an operator who asks for `-p 2` in one repo and `-p 1` in four others has not asked for 6 — they have asked for 6 *drivers*, each free to spawn a toolchain that itself claims every core.

Measured on this host 2026-08-20. A 14-physical-core machine, five concurrent runs, **load average 62 — 4.4x oversubscribed**. In `cuneiform` the consequence was precise and expensive: a healthy full merge gate there is **158 seconds** (`cuneiform/340-build-cache-hygiene`, and that repo's own cache checker still reports the tree healthy at 10,260 dep files), yet `353-console-linear-order` spent a **~5 hour iteration whose entire output was** *"Gate is still on `engine-build`, the first of nine. Waiting."* The same agent recorded the cause without recognising it: **three concurrent `verify.sh` processes**, each invoking an uncapped `cargo` that asks for all 14 cores. Across 37 iterations, **12 consumed 85% of 23.6 hours**, and every one of the longest began with all of its stories already passing — the clock was in re-verification, not in writing code.

The repo-side half is fixable in the repo and has been (`cuneiform` now caps `[build] jobs`). **The half that belongs here is that chief hands out parallelism it does not own.** `-p` bounds tasklists inside one run; nothing bounds runs against each other, and the resource actually being contended — cores — is a property of the machine, not of a repo.

This is filed as `fix` rather than `feature` deliberately. `-p N` already promises a bound and does not deliver one once a second run exists; a flag whose stated meaning holds only in the single-run case is a defect in the flag.

Do NOT solve this by making chief a scheduler daemon. A run registry already exists — `chief ps` reads live records across every repo — so the cheap version is cooperative: consult what is already recorded, and hold rather than oversubscribe.

userStories.title: A run can see what the machine is already doing
acceptanceCriteria: Chief reads the existing cross-repo run registry — the same records `chief ps` renders — to determine how many agent turns and gates are live on this machine before launching another. No new daemon, no new state store: `ps` already proves the data is there.
A stale record (a driver whose pid is gone) must not count toward the budget. `chief reap` already models this and the same predicate is reused rather than re-derived.
The count is reported in a way an operator can check, so 'why is my run holding' is answerable without reading source.
A test drives fixture run records — including one stale — and asserts the derived count.
userStories.notes: test/concurrency.sh: green — fixture found 1 live run with 1 agent turn and 1 gate, and ignored 1 stale PID record; bash -n, version-bump, doc-sync, and smoke passed. test/ratelimit.sh has an unrelated existing epoch-form fixture failure (agent exited 0, expected 2).

userStories.title: A machine-wide budget bounds concurrency across runs, and defaults to the hardware
acceptanceCriteria: A machine-wide limit bounds concurrent agent turns across ALL runs, configurable and defaulting to something derived from the host's core count rather than a round number. The measured failure was 4.4x oversubscription on 14 cores.

A run that would exceed the budget HOLDS rather than failing or oversubscribing, and says what it is waiting for. Holding is the drain-not-kill behaviour `chief pause` already establishes; a refusal would make a second repo unusable.
`-p N` keeps its meaning WITHIN a run and is additionally clamped by the machine budget. Documented explicitly, because the current flag reads as an absolute bound and is not one.
The budget is opt-outable in one obvious way for an operator who genuinely wants the old behaviour, and the opt-out is recorded in the run's own log so a later investigation can see it was set.
A test starts two fixture runs against a budget of one and asserts the second holds, then proceeds when the first finishes.

userStories.title: Contention is visible where the operator already looks
acceptanceCriteria: `chief ps` shows load average against core count when the machine is oversubscribed. A 6-hour iteration and a 3-minute one look identical in the output today, and the difference was never in the repo.
A tasklist holding on the machine budget renders as a distinct state with its reason — not as generic `pending`, which is what a blocked-on-dependency tasklist already means.

The stall/quiet thresholds account for contention rather than flagging a queued gate as hung. `monitor.sh` already tunes per-phase thresholds against measurements and this is the same idea: a gate waiting for cores is working, and must not be reported as stalled.
Document the failure shape in `docs/reference/` with the numbers, so the next operator reading a slow run checks `uptime` before rebuilding their theory of the repo.
